claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi thin films and nanoribbons possess significant residual stress.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi structures have a high density of surface or interface defects.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi structures have a nanocrystalline grain structure.
Reduced dimensionality, residual stress, and surface or interface defects produce local lattice distortions in FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons.
The local lattice distortions alter magnetic exchange interactions.
The local lattice distortions promote heterogeneous magnetic-domain configurations.
Nanoscale surface effects and processing-induced stress increase domain-wall pinning and local magnetic anisotropy.
Increased domain-wall pinning and local anisotropy broaden magnetic hysteresis.
Increased domain-wall pinning and local anisotropy reduce magnetocaloric efficiency under low applied fields.
A 250–350 °C vacuum anneal for one hour will partially relieve residual stress.
The proposed anneal will promote modest grain coarsening without causing unwanted phase transformations.
Annealing will reduce defect density and produce a more homogeneous magnetic-domain structure.
Annealed samples will have lower coercive fields and narrower hysteresis loops than as-deposited controls.
Annealed samples will exhibit a greater adiabatic temperature change per unit applied field than as-deposited controls.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons show significant hysteresis and diminished magnetocaloric temperature change relative to bulk forms.
Surface and residual-stress effects dominate magnetic behavior in the 10–100 nm thickness or width regime.
Heat-transfer rates inherent to the nanoscale structures limit the magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
The proposed mechanism applies for applied magnetic fields below 500 Oe.
The annealing temperature must remain below the onset of large-scale grain growth or phase separation.
An identically deposited, unannealed sample set serves as the experimental control for the annealed sample set.
